story.headline: Parmelin to leave Federal Council
story.summary: Federal President Guy Parmelin announced he will step down from the Federal Council on 31 December, opening a seat parliament will fill in December.
story.display_body: Federal President Guy Parmelin announced on Friday 2 October that he will step down from the seven-member Federal Council (Switzerland's collegial national executive) on 31 December, triggering a by-election in parliament. The 66-year-old Vaud winegrower, who heads the economics department (EAER) and is serving his second year as rotating Federal President, said the decision has nothing to do with his health — persistent rumours about his back had circulated for years — and that "no one is irreplaceable" and the moment had come "to make way for fresh forces." Elected in December 2015 as the first French-speaking member of the Swiss People's Party (SVP/UDC) ever to sit on the Council, he leaves after 11 years in which he ran the defence and then the economics portfolios; only this week he defended the negotiated social-partner compromise on wage protection and the EU-CH treaty package in parliament. His departure opens a seat the Federal Assembly will fill in a December vote, with the SVP expected to claim it.
story.why: the resignation reshuffles the federal executive just as parliament is handling the Bilaterals III treaty package with the EU and a tariff dispute with Washington — files Parmelin personally carried — and sets off a succession contest for one of the country's seven top jobs.

story.headline: Up to 900,000 Swiss may switch insurer
story.summary: Deloitte estimated up to 900,000 people in Switzerland will change health insurer as 2027 basic-insurance premiums rise about 5 percent.
story.display_body: Up to 900,000 people in Switzerland are likely to switch health insurer this autumn, the consultancy Deloitte estimated in a survey published Friday 2 October, after basic-insurance premiums were set to rise about 5% in 2027. The estimate — a range of roughly 600,000 to 900,000 — rests on a YouGov poll of 1,236 residents conducted in the third quarter of 2026; nearly half said a premium increase of 20 francs a month would prompt them to consider changing provider, and a quarter reported difficulty paying their premiums at all. The 2027 rise, announced by the Federal Office of Public Health in late September, lifts the average monthly premium to about 412 francs, or roughly 19.70 francs more per month.
story.why: switching insurer is the main lever Swiss households have to blunt a premium rise under the country's mandatory private health-insurance system, so a record churn is less a surprise than a measure of how hard the increases are biting — but it does nothing to change the underlying cost of care.

story.headline: Swiss state pensions rise for 2027
story.summary: The Federal Council raised AVS/AI old-age and disability pensions 1.59 percent for 2027, lifting the minimum monthly pension from 1,260 to 1,280 francs.
story.display_body: The Federal Council decided on Friday 2 October to raise state old-age and disability pensions (AVS/AI) by 1.59% from 1 January 2027, lifting the minimum monthly pension from 1,260 to 1,280 francs. The maximum full pension rises from 2,520 to 2,560 francs, and minimum contributions for the self-employed and non-working also edge up; AVS/AI pensions are adjusted roughly every two years to a "mixed index" blending price and wage growth, and were last changed in 2025.
story.why: the adjustment touches every pensioner and contributor in the country, though at 20 francs a month on the minimum it only partly offsets rising living costs and the 2027 health-premium increase.

story.headline: US sends third carrier toward Iran
story.summary: A US official said the United States is deploying a third aircraft carrier group toward Iran as the US-Israel war on Iran enters its eighth month.
story.display_body: A US official told Al Jazeera on Friday 2 October that the United States is sending a third aircraft carrier strike group toward Iran, as the US-Israel war on Iran enters its eighth month. According to the official, the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier group left its San Diego base on Sunday 28 September, followed a day later by the Makin Island amphibious force carrying more than 2,000 Marines; the official framed the roughly 50,000-troop regional build-up, which also includes F-35 jets, as pressure on Tehran. The claim rests on that single unnamed official and the administration's own characterisation of its intent, which it has repeatedly recast over the course of the war.
story.why: concentrating a third carrier in the region raises the military stakes at a moment both sides say they are weighing escalation against renewed diplomacy, but the stated rationale comes from an administration that has framed earlier moves in this war as "final" before continuing them — so the deployment is clearer than the intention behind it.

story.headline: US delivers first F-16Vs to Taiwan
story.summary: The United States delivered the first two of 66 F-16V Block 70 jets to Taiwan under an 8-billion-dollar sale after months of delay.
story.display_body: The United States delivered the first two F-16V Block 70 fighter jets to Taiwan on Friday 2 October, the island's defence ministry said, as Taipei builds up its forces against the threat of a Chinese attack. The aircraft, built by Lockheed Martin, landed at Chihhang air base in Taitung and are the first of 66 jets under an 8-billion-dollar sale approved during Donald Trump's first term; the handover had been delayed for months, amid repeated requests from Beijing that Washington stop arming the island.
story.why: the delivery is a concrete test of the US commitment to arm Taiwan that Taipei has grown anxious about, and lands days after a Trump-Xi summit at which the two sides floated tariff cuts — underscoring how arms sales and trade now pull in opposite directions.

story.headline: Ethiopia and Eritrea sever ties
story.summary: Ethiopia expelled ten Eritrean diplomats and closed its embassy in Asmara over renewed Tigray fighting; Eritrea reciprocated, unwinding the 2018 peace.
story.display_body: Ethiopia and Eritrea severed diplomatic relations on Thursday 1 October, after Addis Ababa expelled ten Eritrean diplomats and shut its embassy in Asmara, accusing its northern neighbour of "direct and indirect acts of hostility" tied to renewed fighting in Ethiopia's Tigray region. Ethiopia's foreign ministry declared the ten diplomats persona non grata and gave them 48 hours to leave; hours later Eritrea called the move "absurd" and said it had "no option but to reciprocate in kind." The rupture unwinds the 2018 rapprochement between the two countries — the peace deal for which Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed won the 2019 Nobel Peace Prize.
story.why: Eritrea and Ethiopia fought a border war that killed tens of thousands, and a formal break between them as the Tigray conflict reignites raises the risk of a wider Horn of Africa war drawing in outside actors.

story.headline: Russian drones shut Kyiv bridges
story.summary: New Russian drone attacks killed at least one person in Kyiv and forced several Dnipro bridges, including the Southern and Paton bridges, to close.
story.display_body: New Russian drone attacks on Kyiv killed at least one person and forced several bridges over the Dnipro River to close on Friday 2 October, the city's authorities said. Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the Southern (Pivdennyi) Bridge — which carries road traffic and a metro line and had been struck twice in two days — was completely shut, as was the Paton Bridge; Russia's defence ministry said it had targeted a Dnipro bridge used for military purposes. Only eight bridges link Kyiv's western and eastern banks, so closures snarl civilian movement across the capital.
story.why: striking the capital's river crossings widens Russia's campaign against infrastructure as winter approaches, after a brief September truce lapsed and the fighting resumed.

story.headline: Latvia votes amid Russia fears
story.summary: Latvia holds a Saeima parliamentary election on 3 October, with national security and relations with Russia dominating the campaign.
story.display_body: Latvia holds a parliamentary (Saeima) election on Saturday 3 October, with national security and the country's relationship with Russia dominating the campaign. Most leading parties are running on defence pledges after a series of drone incursions into Baltic airspace in recent months; NATO has reinforced the alliance's eastern flank, including German Eurofighter jets stationed about 60 kilometres from Riga.
story.why: the vote is an early read on how Baltic electorates are responding to heightened Russian pressure and the economic cost of cutting remaining ties with Moscow.
